d.title: The redundancy, measured on real speech
d.caption: The filterbank's triangles overlap by construction, so neighbouring bands measure overlapping slices of the same spectrum — and on 3.4 seconds of real speech adjacent bands correlate at **0.9524**. The DCT is an orthogonal rotation into a basis where that structure is largely gone, cutting the mean absolute correlation by 62%. Nothing is lost in the rotation itself; it is invertible. What loses information is the truncation that follows.

d.title: Energy compaction, and why thirteen
d.caption: The energy piles into the first few coefficients, so truncation is cheap. **The first coefficient alone holds 71% of it** — essentially overall loudness, which is why it is often discarded for speaker-independent work. Thirteen reach 98.22%, and reconstructing the log-mel from them costs a mean absolute error of 2.76% of the feature's range. The classic choice of 13 is well judged rather than arbitrary.

d.title: Low coefficients are the envelope, high ones are the pitch
d.caption: The cepstrum is a spectrum of a log spectrum, so its low coefficients describe slow variation *across frequency* — the broad shape of the vocal tract's response, which is what determines the phoneme. High coefficients describe rapid variation, which is the harmonic comb of the glottal pulse train: pitch. Truncating to 13 therefore keeps **what was said** and discards **who said it and at what pitch** — exactly right for speaker-independent recognition and exactly wrong for speaker identification.

nodes.label: A spectrum of a log spectrum

d.title: Size is the only argument the DCT has left
d.caption: Decorrelation mattered when the acoustic model was a Gaussian mixture with diagonal covariance, because a diagonal matrix assumes the features are independent and correlated log-mel bands violate that. A neural network has no such assumption, so the rotation buys nothing — and the truncation now **costs** information the network could have used. What remains is the byte count, and it matters on a microcontroller running a wake word in a few kilobytes of RAM.

d.title: Three ways to turn audio into text
d.caption: The row that decides most real choices is the first. CTC's conditional independence per frame is what lets it stream cheaply and also what leaves it with no internal language model — it cannot represent that `u` follows `q`. RNN-T fixes that structurally and still streams, which is why it is the on-device standard; an attention decoder is the most accurate and cannot stream at all, because its encoder is bidirectional over the whole utterance.

d.title: The streaming question eliminates options before anything else does
d.caption: Ask whether text must appear before the utterance finishes, and most of the design space closes immediately — which is why this is the first question rather than an accuracy comparison. The fourth branch is the one people forget: forced alignment wants CTC specifically, because its monotonic lattice hands you frame timings directly, and that is how subtitle timings and phoneme boundaries get produced.

d.title: The collapse rule, in the order that matters
d.caption: Squeeze repeated symbols **first**, then remove blanks — and the order is the whole trick. Doing it the other way round would make `a a` and `a` indistinguishable, so there would be no way to spell a doubled letter. The blank is therefore not silence; it is a separator that lets `a - a` survive as `aa` while `a a` becomes `a`.

nodes.label: a a - b b  ->  a b
a - a b  ->  a a b

d.title: All five paths that collapse to `ab`, enumerated
d.caption: Three frames over `{a, b, blank}` give 27 possible paths and exactly five of them collapse to the target. CTC sums **all five** rather than picking the best — which is the whole difference between it and a forced alignment, and the reason it needs no frame-level labels. The total, 0.5100, is the number the lattice must reproduce.

d.title: The forward lattice, every cell
d.caption: The target is padded with blanks to `- a - b -`, and each cell holds the summed probability of every path reaching that state at that frame. The answer is the last two cells added: 0.1400 + 0.3700 = **0.5100**, identical to the enumeration. The lattice is not an approximation — it is the same sum, computed column by column because reaching a state depends only on the previous frame.

d.title: What matching PyTorch actually confirms
d.caption: Agreement to float64 round-off is a stronger check than it looks, because it tests four separate things at once — and three of them are conventions rather than arithmetic. A hand-written lattice that is mathematically perfect still disagrees if the blank index or the tensor layout is wrong, so this is the test to run before trusting your own implementation on anything real.

d.title: Forward times backward is where the gradient comes from
d.caption: The forward variable is the probability of **reaching** a state; a symmetric backward pass gives the probability of **completing** the target from it. Their product at a state and frame is the total probability of all valid paths passing through that cell — so dividing by the sequence's total probability gives the posterior that this frame emitted this symbol, and that posterior is the gradient. Which is why CTC produces the characteristic spiky alignment: the posterior concentrates on a few frames per symbol.

d.title: Why the dynamic program was a contribution and not a formulation
d.caption: At three frames the enumeration is 27 paths and the lattice is 15 cells — no reason to prefer either. At a realistic 300 frames the enumeration is **1.4 × 10¹⁴³ paths**, vastly more than the atoms in the observable universe, while the lattice still needs 1,500 cells. And the alphabet here is three symbols; a real character set makes the exponential base far larger while leaving the lattice linear.

d.title: What streaming costs, as a right-context dial
d.caption: A streaming encoder must commit before hearing what follows, and speech is full of cases where a later word disambiguates an earlier one. Right context is therefore the direct trade: 320–640 ms buys most of the accuracy back for a latency most users do not notice, and the two-pass arrangement — stream a fast answer, then rescore the whole utterance — is what phones actually ship.

d.title: Whisper's thesis, which is about data rather than architecture
d.caption: Architecturally it is a plain encoder-decoder transformer — unremarkable, and deliberately so. The claim is that **scale and diversity beat clever objectives**: 680,000 hours of weakly-labelled multilingual web audio, with no pretext task at all, produces robustness that the self-supervised approaches of 6.4 were designed to buy. The cost is in the failure modes of §04, which are data artefacts rather than architectural limits.

d.title: Three failure modes, and the fix for each
d.caption: All three are consequences of how it was trained rather than bugs. The first is the one that reaches production most often: given a window with no speech, the decoder still produces fluent text — frequently a sign-off phrase learned from YouTube subtitles — and it does so confidently, so nothing downstream can tell.

d.title: Five decoding choices, from cheapest to most product-specific
d.caption: The third row is the correction most CTC implementations need: plain beam search scores different frame alignments of the same text as separate hypotheses, so an apparent width of ten may carry only three or four distinct candidates. **Prefix** beam search merges them and uses the full width on genuinely different text — it is the correct algorithm, not merely a faster one.

d.title: Biasing is information you already have at request time
d.caption: A generic model has never seen your contacts, your playlist names or your part numbers — and those are precisely the words a user most wants recognised. *"Call Aoife"* fails against a general model and succeeds when the beam is boosted toward the contact list injected at session start. No amount of general model improvement substitutes for it, because the information is not in the training data and **is** available at request time.

d.title: The TTS pipeline, stage by stage
d.caption: Four stages, and the first is the one that is pure engineering and gets skipped: `$3.50` has to become *three dollars fifty* before anything acoustic happens, and a model asked to pronounce the raw string will do something arbitrary. The vocoder choice is where the practical trade sits — Griffin-Lim is fast and robotic, WaveNet is excellent and slow, and HiFi-GAN is why neither is the default any more.

d.title: Where it went: audio as tokens
d.caption: A neural codec turns audio into discrete tokens, and a language model over those tokens does TTS. That reframing is what makes **voice cloning from a few seconds of reference audio** fall out for free — the reference is simply a prompt prefix in the token sequence, with no speaker embedding or fine-tuning involved. The same trick underlies speech-to-speech models, where audio tokens go in and audio tokens come out with no text in between.

d.title: The five small models that sit around the recogniser
d.caption: None of these is the ASR model and all of them decide whether the product works. The third row is the one that is routinely confused with the first: VAD asks whether anyone is speaking *now*, endpointing asks whether they have **finished** — a much harder question, because a pause mid-sentence and a pause at the end look identical for the first few hundred milliseconds.

d.title: Five rows that show what WER cannot see
d.caption: Rows 1 and 2 score **identically** — yet dropping `two` from a temperature command changes what the thermostat does, while `degree` for `degrees` changes nothing at all. `mum` to `mom` costs 0.1667 and is completely harmless. And the last row is 3.0000, because insertions divide by the *reference* length, so WER is unbounded above: anyone quoting "97% accurate" from a WER of 0.03 is inverting a quantity that has no complement.

d.title: Four identical meanings, four different numbers
d.caption: Nothing about the recognition changed across these four — only how numbers, punctuation and casing are rendered — and the score moves from 0.0000 to 0.1667. Two systems on the same audio can differ by several points on this alone, which is more than separates many competing models. **Fix one normaliser, publish it, and compare only within it**: a WER quoted without its normalisation scheme is not a comparable number.

d.title: The other metrics, and which one your product cares about
d.caption: Entity error rate is usually the one that matters: a user does not care that the model wrote `mom` for `mum`, and cares enormously whether the phone number survived. It frequently disagrees with WER — a system with worse WER can be clearly better in use because its errors fall on filler words — and RTF against latency disagree the same way, since a buffer leaves RTF flat while time-to-first-token rises.

d.title: Augmentation, and what each technique stands in for
d.caption: Every row is a cheap way to buy a recording condition you cannot collect. SpecAugment is first because it is both the most effective ASR augmentation and **free** — it masks bands of frequency and spans of time in the log-mel, with no audio processing at all. The rest are worth the cost in proportion to how closely they match your deployment: a car wants reverberation and road noise, a phone line wants codec simulation.

The second is silent, which is worse — a frame-count off-by-two misaligns features against labels and the model simply learns less well, with no error anywhere. d.title: Both 16-bit formats, and where the bits went
d.caption: Same 16 bits, allocated differently. Float16 spends more on the mantissa — better precision, and a range topping out at 65,504. Bfloat16 spends more on the exponent, giving **float32's full range** at worse precision. For training, range is the binding constraint: gradients span many orders of magnitude while precision requirements are modest, because the gradient is a noisy estimate anyway. That is the whole reason bf16 needs no loss scaling and fp16 does.

d.title: The scaler is a feedback controller, and its state is a diagnostic
d.caption: It multiplies the loss, checks the gradients for infinities, and on finding any it **skips the step and halves the scale**; after enough clean steps it doubles. So it hunts for the largest scale that does not overflow — which makes its behaviour informative. A scale that stabilises high means fp16 is comfortable; one that keeps halving means the overflow is structural and the problem is upstream. Log the scale, and log the fraction of steps skipped, because silently discarding a large share of your updates looks exactly like slow convergence.

nodes.label: Yes: skip the step, halve the scale
No, for many steps: double it

d.title: The hang, which produces no error at all
d.caption: Training simply stops making progress. No exception, no log line, no crash — the job sits there consuming GPUs until someone notices. The cause is almost always that the ranks **disagree about which collectives to run**, so one waits forever for a partner that never arrives. The discipline is absolute: every rank executes the same collectives in the same order, which makes a `dist.barrier()` inside an `if rank == 0:` branch an instant deadlock.

d.title: A checkpoint that looks fine and cannot be loaded
d.caption: With FSDP or ZeRO each rank holds only part of the parameters, so a naive `state_dict()` on rank 0 saves that rank's fragment — **a file of plausible size that cannot reconstruct the model**. The write also has to be atomic, to a temporary path then renamed, or a crash mid-save overwrites a good checkpoint with a corrupt one. On a multi-week run, discovering this is the worst possible moment to find out, which is why the last step is the one that matters.
